source_read: PMC full text PMC3805449 (J Addict Dis 2013;32(3):231-243), read in the app's browser in my own tab; whole article read (abstract, Introduction, Methods, Discussion and Recommendations with its four subsections, the four case definitions, the causality section with Cases 1 to 4, Conclusions, Appendices A to C, the 19 references) plus the author notes and funding statement, read from the page with a script. Paragraph counts were checked against the page structure with a script: Introduction 3, Scene Investigation 2, Toxicologic Testing 6 plus the nine numbered standards, causality section 23. No tables, figures or supplement. Card check only (the task lists no claims); I read the source and noted my own observations before opening the card.

key_findings.correction: Appendix A lists 2 co-chairs, 10 members and 13 ex officio members (FDA 4, DEA 2, SAMHSA 3, CDC and NCHS 2, NIDA 1, JBS International 1), as the card says. The 19 references also split 8 journal articles and 11 other documents, as design_detail says.
The source says many immunoassays miss toxicologically significant opiates, especially oxycodone and hydromorphone; the rest matches the 1st and 2nd paragraphs.

Standard 2 says admission blood and urine are to be collected and tested 'as opposed to' autopsy specimens, when applicable and available. The card's '(not only autopsy)' turns a preference into an addition. Corrected: test admission rather than autopsy blood and urine where applicable and available. The other eight points match.

Matches. The sentence about adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use follows the NCHS description, but its referent ('This definition') could be either NCHS's category or the panel's. The panel's own Includes list already names adverse drug reactions and effects, so the content is the same either way.

Paragraphs 1 to 4 of the causality section as stated (synthesis; pre-terminal events, tolerance, methadone accumulating during induction, loss of tolerance after prison or hospital; competing causes; mixed intoxications).

X42 with T40.5 against F14, the five and four phrases, and the advice on wording and on 'overdose' are in paragraphs 10 to 12. The Appendix B entry 'Overdose (OD)' sits under the Drug Poisoning heading.

Paragraphs 13 to 16. One small embellishment: the case does not say 'night'. It describes an episode of drug use with friends, after which he went to sleep and could not be woken the next day. The note on ethanol is right: the comment invokes a high concentration of 'the opioid or ethanol', and no ethanol is reported.

reporting_issues.note: Re-found independently. Add: the circumstantial-evidence sentence in the drug-detected definition even ends 'to certify the death as a drug poisoning death', so it appears to have been copied from definition 1-a.

Nuance: two ex officio members (Campbell and Lubran) are from the Division of Pharmacologic Therapies of SAMHSA's Center for Substance Abuse Treatment, the federal office overseeing opioid treatment programmes. They are regulators rather than clinicians, so 'none described as working in addiction treatment' stands, but the Introduction's wording may refer to them.
Re-found independently. The author notes also say all panel members 'had access to the data', in a paper with no data.

'Without explanation' is too strong. Case 2 itself gives no reason, but its scenario (methadone started 4 days earlier) is the one the 2nd paragraph of the causality section describes: long half-life drugs such as methadone accumulating to toxic concentrations in the first days of treatment, before steady state or tolerance. The comment speaks of tolerance to 'the drug's effects', meaning methadone. Corrected issue: Case 2 does not explain why years of other opioid analgesics conferred no tolerance to methadone (the induction-period rationale is left implicit). In both cases tolerance is inferred from history, not measured, and in both the inference supports attribution. The consequence stands.
The definitions give drug-caused (with drug-poisoning as a subcategory) and drug-detected; no separate 'contributing' category exists.
All six typographical errors and the Consensus Panel / Expert Panel alternation are present. Two more: 'causes about death' and 'did not contribute the death' (Case 4 comment).

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' narrative-review checklist with an overall 'high' fits, since no recommendation is linked to graded evidence. I checked the domain-3 note: reference 5 has co-chair Goldberger as an author and reference 14 is panel member Hanzlick's book. The reasoning's limits on what the statement may be cited for are right.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair for a consensus statement. One reading point: the Conclusions sentence ('Concise, scientifically accurately, universally accepted case definitions like those presented here can address...') can also be read as aspirational (definitions of this kind, once accepted, could address the distinction), so 'no evidence of acceptance is offered' should be framed as a possible overstatement rather than a plain claim of acceptance.

missed: The scene-investigation recommendations appear only in the exposure field, not as a key finding: inventory the drugs at the scene to estimate the amount taken; for controlled prescription drugs, request the state prescription-monitoring records (prescription history, use without a prescription, tolerance); in methadone or buprenorphine deaths, contact local opioid treatment programmes (Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). They bear directly on how a death is investigated, one of the new section's questions.

Standard 2 recommends testing admission (pre-death) specimens, while the drug-detected definition is built on post-mortem testing and excludes deaths whose toxicology was done before death by hospital staff. The statement does not say whether a drug found only in admission specimens tested by the medical examiner's laboratory makes a death drug-detected.

Toxicologic Testing, 3rd paragraph: the panel asks that measurements be judged on whether they can separate acute from chronic use (free against glucuronidated metabolites, by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry). This is not in the card's findings.
